title: Searching Algorithms: Binary vs Simple Search
summary: Two ways to find an item: linear (simple) search checks every item one by one, which is O(n); binary search halves a sorted list each step, which is O(log n). Your first look at Big-O and why algorithm choice matters in interviews. The step-by-step arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Write linear and binary search in Python, count their steps, and explain when binary search is allowed and why it's faster.

steps.title: Read the lesson
steps.detail: Read Linear vs Binary Search on the curriculum site. Note binary search's must-have: the list has to be sorted.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain the phone-book idea of binary search out loud.

steps.title: Trace binary search by hand
steps.detail: On paper, search for 30 in [7, 10, 15, 18, 22, 30, 42]. Write left, right and mid for each round. Then count how many checks linear search would need for the same target.
steps.doneWhen: Binary search finds 30 in 2 checks; linear search needs 6.

steps.title: Skim the assignment README
steps.detail: The curriculum lists Linear vs Binary (three scenarios: unsorted numbers, sorted words, last occurrence; each returns the index and the step count) and a Refactor task on your earlier work. Wait for Slack before forking.
steps.doneWhen: You know the three scenarios and what each function must return.

concepts.meaning: Check each item in order until you find it. Works on any list.
Check the middle, throw away the half that can't hold the target, and repeat. Needs a sorted list.
How the work grows as the input grows, in the worst case.
1,000,000 items: up to 1,000,000 checks vs about 20.
